newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU, ERM hopefuls and budgets dominate fall season.
newsitem.headline: EMU, ERM hopefuls and budgets dominate fall season.

text.p: The European Union will be under intense pressure between now and the end of the year to deliver progress on a series of issues related to economic and monetary union (EMU).
A budget stability pact, a new Exchange Rate Mechanism and the legal underpinings of a common currency will be addressed by the European Commission during the first half of this month.
Together with the views of the European Monetary Institute, the conclusions will form the basis for discussion among EU finance ministers meeting in Dublin on September 21.
The unveiling of such views, however, comes at a most inauspicious time.

Despite unwavering political commitment, underscored this past weekend by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac in Bonn, doubts over the strength of Europe's economies and the ability of governments to control public spending have come to dominate the minds of investors.

A majority of EU governments will release details of their 1997 budgets over the coming weeks. Attention will be particularly focused on France, with Prime Minister Alain Juppe scheduled to announce the government's plan on September 10.
Separately, there is growing speculation that Finland will join the ERM relatively soon. Its entry could come at just about any weekend.
Regarding the three main areas in EMU under discussion, here is a brief summary of where negotiations stand.

BUDGET STABILITY PACT -- A German initiative designed to enforce budget discipline among EMU participants, the primary obstacle is how to incorporate penalities in an automatic fashion against governments which let their deficits rise.
While the Maastricht treaty already allows for fines on those with deficits above 3.0 percent of GDP, the procedure is considered cumbersome and without much bite.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel wants the review process sped up, and the Commission has put forward a compromise which seeks to streamline the process. How to accomplish this, however, is a bit tricky given the treaty's legal constraints.

As Werner Becker of Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt puts it: "The key point is how to fit the stability pact into a legal framework." EU officials say the most reasonable option would be to have secondary legislation which includes Waigel's plan.
The Commission will likely put forward its own thoughts next week.

ERM II - Unlike the present currency grid where currencies are bi-laterally aligned against each other, the new proposal will put the single currency as the anchor and all currencies not in the EMU area will, if their governments want, trade against it in relatively wide and flexible bands.
The voluntary nature of a new ERM is considered essential.

"My view is that countries will not be forced to join the ERM but I think the EU will say that any country that wishes to enter EMU in the future will have to be a member," says Charles Goodhart of the London School of Economics.
Still unclear, however, is the role the European Central Bank (ECB) will play in supporting currencies outside the grid should they come under speculative attack.

There is a strong desire to place limits on intervention and many want the ECB to have a say in initiating parity changes should the need arise. But such a proposal runs into questions about political sovereignty and no one is yet certain what kind of compromise will be forthcoming.

Commission officials say they are less involved in this area, with the EMI taking the lead role. It is less likely that the Commission will deliver a paper on the subject ahead of the Dublin informal ECOFIN on September 21.
LEGAL FRAMEWORK - The issue of contract continuity has been uppermost in the minds of financial markets and the Commission has tried to assauge such worries through numerous proposals.

The major concern is what legal standing bondholders have, for example, when a contract denominated in a national currency matures after the start of EMU in 1999. Some investors want every contingency covered in EU legislation, but many say that such blanket coverage is virtually impossible.

Another question mark is when the legal framework is enacted. Under the treaty the EU may have to delay a final decision until 1998. For investors, there is a strong desire to have such issues clarified as soon as possible.
The Commission has circulated several drafts among the legal community and reaction so far has been favourable.
Officials say the Commission should formally put forward its views next week.

On all three issues the objective is to complete as much work as possible ahead of the Dublin summit in December. It is expected that work on the stability pact and the legal framework should be largely completed by then.
The nuts and bolts of a new ERM, however, is less certain, since it is in the hands of the EMI and will likely involve prolonged discussions among central bankers.
